title: Mechanistic modeling of critical network transitions in neuroinflammation
summary: Multiple sclerosis is an inflammatory disease in which an autoimmune reaction destroys nerve cells in the central nervous system, i.e., the brain and spinal cord. The consequences of this inflammation can include permanent physical disabilities such as visual impairment, paralysis, or sensory disturbances. The disease progresses in episodes, especially in the early stages, which means that acute inflammation occurs spontaneously in the central nervous system. In clinical practice, it is particularly important to recognize an episode early and reliably in order to prevent permanent damage to the nerve tissue through targeted therapy. Clinically, it is not always possible to identify a relapse event with certainty. In such cases, additional non-clinical parameters would be helpful in supporting a treatment decision. This raises the question of whether there is a parameter that can be easily determined from blood and used to reliably detect acute inflammation in the central nervous system. The observation of individual biomarkers has so far failed to show a reliable correlation with acute relapses. Our hypothesis is therefore that various biomarkers shift during the course of an acute relapse and that it is possible to identify a pattern characteristic of an acute relapse by determining several parameters. The biomarkers are determined from blood. Samples are therefore taken at the time of the acute relapse, after one month, and after three to six months. In order to objectively determine whether a past relapse in the central nervous system is actually detectable after three months, patients undergo an MRI scan. This can reveal any new scarring in the central nervous system. At the same time, the above-mentioned markers are determined from the serum of patients with multiple sclerosis who have not had a clinical relapse. These patients serve as a control group.
conditions: Multiple sclerosis with a predominantly relapsing-remitting course and acute exacerbation

interventions.name: Determination of various biomarkers from the serum of patients with multiple sclerosis at the time of an acute relapse and one and three months later. Magnetic resonance imaging after three months to objectively assess a relapse event.
One-time determination of the biomarkers from the serum of patients with multiple sclerosis without acute relapse.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Primary diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS)
Clinical suspicion of acute relapse or appropriate age, gender, and immunotherapy for patients in the acute relapse group
Exclusion criteria:
Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
